subject: Prior for shrinking group-level standard deviation to overall standard deviation

messages.author: fa6f5d4c13c0cca5
messages.subject: Prior for shrinking group-level standard deviation to overall standard deviation
parts:
This is question is probably more about statistics than Stan specifically.  

I'm interested in modeling some data where each group's standard deviation is allowed to differ, but assumed to share some common information. Essentially, I'm looking for a prior that shrinks the group level variance towards the overall variance.  I've read a number of papers on hierarchical shrinkage priors (e.g., the horseshoe prior), which allow a few parameters to have a large standard deviation while shrinking most of the others to zero, but these don't really have the behavior for which I'm looking.

I've considered a possible candidate, but I'm unsure as to if it actually makes any sort of sense. 

y[i,j]    ~ Normal(mu[j], sigma[j])
sigma[j]  = lambda[j] * tau
tau       ~ half-t(nu_tau, 0, s_tau)
lambda[j] ~ log_normal(0, epsilon)
epsilon   ~ half-t(nu_epsilon, 0, s_epsilon)
mu[j]     ~ ... However you wish to model the means

The s and nu variables are fixed hyperparameters, and j represents a group. The idea is that as epsilon -> 0, lambda[j] -> 1 and sigma[j] -> tau.  

I've run a few simulations (attached). The estimates for tau and epsilon are vague and have an effective sample size that's usually around 10% of of the number of retained iterations; lambda and raw_log_lambda have an n_eff in the same range.  Despite this, it does a very good job at estimating sigma, with n_eff equal to the number of iterations. PP checks also appear to be performing well.  There don't appear to be any convergence issues.

Could anyone here with a better statistical understanding than I have comment as to whether this seems like a reasonable prior?  I'm also somewhat confused as to how sigma can have such a high effective sample size when its components (tau, epsilon, lambda) do not.  Does anyone have any suggestions for reparameterizing the model to deal with these issues?  

Thank you

Model code, same as that which is attached:
// hierStDevShrinkage.stan
data{
  int N;
  int nGroup;
  int<lower=1,upper=nGroup> groupID[N];
  vector[N] y;
  
  real s_epsilon;
  real s_tau;
  real nu_epsilon;
  real nu_tau;
}
parameters{
  // Non-central parameterization of lambda
  vector[nGroup] raw_log_lambda; // normal(0,1)
  real<lower=0> tau; // overall standard deviation
  real<lower=0> epsilon; // shrinkage parameter
}
model{
  // Priors
  raw_log_lambda ~ normal(0,1);
  tau ~ student_t(nu_tau, 0, s_tau);
  epsilon ~ student_t(nu_epsilon, 0, s_epsilon);
  
  //Likelihood
  y ~ normal(0, (tau * exp(raw_log_lambda * epsilon))[groupID]);
}
generated quantities{
  vector[nGroup] lambda;
  vector[nGroup] sigma;
  vector[N] yNew;
 
  lambda = exp(raw_log_lambda * epsilon);
  sigma = tau * lambda;
  for(i in 1:N)
    yNew[i] = normal_rng(0, sigma[groupID[i]]);
}

> On Sep 3, 2016, at 8:07 PM, Christopher Peterson <christopher...@gmail.com> wrote:
>
> This is question is probably more about statistics than Stan specifically.
>
> I'm interested in modeling some data where each group's standard deviation is allowed to differ, but assumed to share some common information. Essentially, I'm looking for a prior that shrinks the group level variance towards the overall variance. I've read a number of papers on hierarchical shrinkage priors (e.g., the horseshoe prior), which allow a few parameters to have a large standard deviation while shrinking most of the others to zero, but these don't really have the behavior for which I'm looking.
>
> I've considered a possible candidate, but I'm unsure as to if it actually makes any sort of sense.
>
> y[i,j] ~ Normal(mu[j], sigma[j])
> sigma[j] = lambda[j] * tau
> tau ~ half-t(nu_tau, 0, s_tau)
> lambda[j] ~ log_normal(0, epsilon)
> epsilon ~ half-t(nu_epsilon, 0, s_epsilon)
> mu[j] ~ ... However you wish to model the means
>
> The s and nu variables are fixed hyperparameters, and j represents a group. The idea is that as epsilon -> 0, lambda[j] -> 1 and sigma[j] -> tau.

epsilon won't go to 0 as the scale and d.o.f. of tau is fixed.

Whether this makes sense as model for your scales sigma[j] depends
on the application area. This isn't a one-size-fits-all kind of
problem any more than other aspects of regressions.

> I've run a few simulations (attached). The estimates for tau and epsilon are vague and have an effective sample size that's usually around 10% of of the number of retained iterations; lambda and raw_log_lambda have an n_eff in the same range. Despite this, it does a very good job at estimating sigma, with n_eff equal to the number of iterations. PP checks also appear to be performing well. There don't appear to be any convergence issues.
>
> Could anyone here with a better statistical understanding than I have comment as to whether this seems like a reasonable prior? I'm also somewhat confused as to how sigma can have such a high effective sample size when its components (tau, epsilon, lambda) do not.

This is an identifiability issue. If there are many ways parameters
theta1 and theta2 can lead to the same theta3 = f(theta1, theta2),
you can get theta3 with high n_eff even if theta1 and theta2 have
low n_eff.

Because sigma[j] = lambda[j] * tau,
you can multiply lambda by a constant C and divide tau by C and get the
same answer for sigma. You're controlling this non-identifiability by
centering the lambdas, but Lognormal and Student-t are not going to
be particularly strong, especially as you allow the scale of lambda
to vary as epsilon. This isn't wrong but can lead to low effective
sample sizes and you should see banana-like pair plots between lambda[j] and
tau and also high correlation among the lambda[j] (the funnel problem you
get with any hierarchical model).
> Does anyone have any suggestions for reparameterizing the model to deal with these issues?

It can help to use the non-centered parameterization for lambda to
deal with the funnel-like issue. It's just the usual one on the log scale.

It might also help to add an intercept term to the sigma[j] instead of
modeling them purely multiplicatively, though that can sometimes lead
to more identifiability problems.

- Bob

messages.author: 3f37be0cf708d442
messages.subject: Re: Prior for shrinking group-level standard deviation to overall standard deviation
parts:
Not sure if this helps, but here is what worked for me.

The idea is to use a gamma distribution to model group
specific sigmas, and to use the non-centered parameterization
version of the cauchy to model the mean and the variance
of the gamma distribution.

parameters {
  ...
  real<lower=0, upper=pi()/2> sigma_mu_unif;
  real<lower=0, upper=pi()/2> sigma_sigma_unif;
  real<lower=0> sigma[M];
}
transformed parameters {
  real<lower=0> sigma_mu;
  real<lower=0> sigma_sigma;
  ...
  sigma_mu <- 5 * tan(sigma_mu_unif);
  sigma_sigma <- 2.5 * tan(sigma_sigma_unif);
}
model {
  ...
  // sigma_sigma_unif ~ unif(...) can and should be omitted
  sigma ~ gamma(sigma_mu^2/sigma_sigma^2, sigma_mu/sigma_sigma^2);
  ...
}



the standard deviations for the prior of the mean and sd 
of the gamma are 5 and 2.5, respectively. One might want to 
adjust that to the scale of predictors and outcome.

(I was modeling the overdispersion parameter of the 
negative binomial, but this should work just as well 
for the variance).

Guido
